utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I apologise that we were a few minutes late coming into court. If I could remind you, Mr. Limaj, of the affirmation that you took at the beginning of your evidence. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm eager to begin but Mr. Mansfield has an issue to raise before we begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield. I'm sorry I didn't notice you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't actually intending to raise it at this juncture, but I can indicate what it is, namely that on Thursday last, we were provided with a list of exhibits that the Prosecution may use in cross-examination. And attached to the list -- and there's no objection to that, they're all in evidence and so forth, obviously. But attached to it is a document which reproduces sections of a book, and I think as far as I can tell, all the sections which come under the various tabs, 2, 3, 4, 5, well, except perhaps 5 doesn't but 4, are excerpts from this book. I think you may have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A document has just been put in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, starting with tab 1, you will then see a series of further dividers, and these are excerpts from this book. And you will see in tab 1 that it was published some time ago, 2001, and is headed basically "The project for the creation of the editorial board for the publication of the monograph on the martyrs of the Kosovo Liberation Army was approved and confirmed by..." and then there's a list, and Fatmir Limaj's name is about halfway down the list on the following page. And then under various headings of individuals under the tabs there is a narrative relating to that individual, Sadik Shala being the first one. I was intending to raise it at the point and if the Prosecution decided they did wish to use this document. However I'm perfectly happy to indicate the objection now so it may be considered. There is no issue but that this document as a whole has plainly been in the possession of the Prosecution for some time. It's not a recent revelation as far as we can tell. No one's suggesting they've only just found it. And clearly had they wished to use this as part of their case, in other words to rely upon this document, then they should have disclosed it a long time ago, and furthermore, obviously have led it in some form or another or adduced it as part of their case. They haven't done either of those things. This isn't a matter that has been disclosed before, and plainly it hasn't been used in any other way as part of their case. It's difficult in those circumstances to see if, in fact, a document of this kind which has been in existence for some time isn't being relied on by the Prosecution quite how they wish to now rely on it. And obviously Mr. Whiting will be able to indicate what the is basis here. But as far as one can see if it's not reliable enough to be used as part of their case, this kind of document, then it's difficult to see how at this stage reliance is suddenly going to be made upon this document. If in fact it's intended to not put it into evidence, and I understand that may be the case, it's not intended to put it into evidence, then its status becomes even less, we would say, either reliable or relevant. In other words, if it's just a matter of saying, "Well, here's this document. We don't rely on it but what do you say about it," then it really has, we would say, peripheral or marginal consequence in relation to these proceedings. But in any event, we say, there is and fundamental principle here. The fundamental principle is, we say, that any matter that the Prosecution wishes to use for whatever purpose in cross-examination should be disclosed in advance. There are exceptions plainly to that, but even those are circumscribed quite carefully. Plainly, if something arises ex improviso, the Prosecution, for example, who may not have reasonably anticipated what has arisen ex improviso, may wish to rebut that matter and of course that's a well known procedure. But that doesn't seem to be what is being sought here. There is an alternative route which is the Prosecution may reopen their case. That again doesn't seem to be what is being requested here, because again, they would be entitled to reopen their case if they could show this wasn't a matter that couldn't have been not only foreseen but have been discovered with due diligence in time for the end of the Prosecution case. Well, that isn't the situation either. There then really remains only two other possibilities. One is in relation to credibility. They might be entitled, provided under the Rules that it is relevant and plainly relates to something that has arisen in chief, then it may possible on a matter of credit although the authorities indicate, I think without exception, that if they're going to do that, 24 hours' notice has to be given at least before the witness is actually called. So in order to do this, they would have had to do it well before Mr. Limaj went into the witness box. Now, may we say on this front we have undertaken not to speak to Mr. Limaj once he went into the witness box, so we haven't. We haven't seen him. We haven't spoken to him, and we haven't given him the list of exhibits, and we haven't told him about this particular exhibit either. So he knows nothing of this. And so certainly so far as the issue of credibility is concerned, there should have been plenty of opportunity for him to consider it. And the fundamental principle which Your Honours will be familiar with is basically an equality of arms. The Prosecution plainly have -- and that's the basis of disclosure, of course, as well -- if a more facilities than the Defence and therefore to equate the matter it is necessary where the Prosecution have is a document they're seeking to use that at least if its credibility there is an opportunity for a defendant to consider what the material is that is about to be used. Well, of course that hasn't happened here. So credibility is one way. The other is, of course, refreshing memory. Well, it's a bit difficult since it's not suggest as far as I know that this is a reliable document. No one is suggesting that it is no doubt they would have used it as part of their case. And it's at the moment difficult to see whether this is a document which actually refreshes any memory since it doesn't appear that it's clear that it was written by or compiled by Mr. Limaj at a time when these were matters within his knowledge, in other words, the usual kind of refreshing-of- memory document. Therefore, none of the usual routes, we would say, apply in this case for even raising this document at this stage in this way whilst he's in the witness box. And may we say also as a general point that applies to I think this material as a whole is that looking at it, generally speaking, it deals with many -- or purports to deal with many events which you've heard a great deal about and names of people, for example Ismet Jashari and so on, and dates are in here of that been spoken about many, many times. Now, if this is being used as a historical document purported to come from the KLA and of importance to the Crown [sic] we say, of course, it should have been led. And they can't have been taken by surprise because without rehearsing in great detail, there was a pre-trial brief in which matters of a general kind were set out for the Prosecution relating to the course of events, and more particularly before Mr. Limaj went in the witness box they were provided, as they are entitled to, to a summary of the main features of his evidence. So they knew perfectly well the parameters of what he was going to speak about. And of course there has been cross-examination in the case on various matters relating to that pre-trial brief as well as the summary provided to the Prosecution just before he gave evidence. So we say there's been plenty of opportunity for this document to be provided. In fairness - and that's really the bottom line, in fairness to this defendant - we're not here attempting to ambush people. We're attempting, as you're only too aware, to reach the truth in a fair and proper way. And of course I don't know the questions that are going to be asked, but Rule 66(B) obviously, again, sets the criteria that they must relate to the Defence case questions or of course the Prosecution case, and plainly withholding this sort of material in the context of that Rule could be construed as -- as the ambush approach to that. So I would ask if it's necessary to have time that this matter is obviously resolved now if the Prosecution are wanting to use this document within the near future. I apologise for doing it in this way at this stage. I anticipate it had might arise later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, when did you say you first received this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I think it was last Thursday. Yes. Yes, it was -- well, I don't know -- it came into my hands about the end of his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that saying it wasn't last Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: My record -- I'm doing it to have the top of my head. I'm fairly sure it came in my hands on Thursday afternoon. The precise point on Thursday afternoon I can't remember. But certainly before we finished Thursday afternoon I had it in my hands but not before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything submit, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I join in the remarks made by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a few words about the document in question. The document is a -- is a book. It's actually a book in four volumes publicly available. It's a public-source document. The document was in the possession of the OTP for some time. However, it was not translated until -- or let's say portions it have were not translated until very recently. I only got the translations that I would like to rely on literally within the last week. And it was only -- I would say, the relevance of the documents only became clear to me after the -- or let's say during the testimony of Mr. Limaj. But more importantly, the -- I think the law is quite clear on this issue. The Prosecution is not intending -- And I say that as a preliminary remark only to make the point that the Prosecution is not trying to ambush here. We weren't holding back this document to drop it on the accused after he testified. It's something that we only became aware of within the last week, or at least its importance. But with respect to the law, the law is quite clear on this point that -- because we are not intending to exhibit this document. We're using it only to -- for cross-examination purposes to challenge the credibility of the witness, to put it to him and to see what his response is to the documents. And I would draw the Court's attention to the Appeals Court judgement in Rutaganda. I've actually made copies I can distribute or ask Mr. Younis to distribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Included in the packet are two decisions the Rutaganda Appeals judgement and a judgement -- judgement from the -- or a decision, rather, from the Milosevic case from fairly recently ago. The Rutaganda Appeals judgement, the case number is ICTR-96-3-A. The number is from the 26 of May, 2003. It's the second document in the packet. I've only produced a few pages of the decision, but I would draw the Court's attention to the paragraph 280 and I would submit that it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: 280. And I would submit that the discussion and decision there is directly on point. In that case, the Prosecution provided -- the appellant testified. The Prosecution provided the Defence with some open-source documents or - at least some of them appear to be open source, if not all of them - open source documents to the Defence after -- after his direct examination and sought to use those documents in the cross-examination. The Prosecution was allowed to do so by the Court. It was an issue on appeal, and the Appeals Court found that there was no error. The Appeals Court went even further and found that there was no error in admitting some if not all of the documents into evidence. And -- but certainly there was no error in the Prosecution using the documents to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any particular passage you rely on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. The background is set out in the preliminary paragraphs following from 280, but drawing the Court's attention to paragraph 284. The Court says: "Considering that the photographs, the press clippings and the articles of association of RTLM boarded on issues that had been raised by the appellant during examination-in-chief, the Appeals Chamber considers that the Trial Chamber had the discretion to admit them during cross-examination of the appellant." And I would note that in paragraph 280 the appellant made the same arguments that the Defence has made here today. And then paragraph 287 also says: "Therefore in the opinion of the Appeals Chamber, the appellant has not demonstrated that the Trial Chamber erred by admitting the photographs contained in the publication entitled 'Rwanda, les medias du genocide' which would afford the Prosecution the opportunity to rebut the allegations made by the appellant during his cross-examination." Here, as I've said, I don't anticipate seeking to exhibit the documents. That's not the purpose of putting them to the witness. Of course if he adopted them, there might arise the possibility that the documents should be exhibited, but I'm not even sure if he adopted them that that would be necessary. I would draw the Court's attention also to the Milosevic decision which I have provided from the 17th of May, 2005. This decision is concerned in particular to paragraph -- paragraphs 10 and 11 of the decision. This decision is concerned primarily with the Prosecution seeking to admit documents during cross-examination during the Defence case. Again, that's not what the Prosecution seeks to do here, but no -- there is no issue raised whatsoever about -- about the Prosecution using documents in its cross-examination that have not been previously disclosed. The decision in the Milosevic cites and quotes from in paragraph 10 an oral decision in the Hadzihasanovic case. In that case, the issue arose of putting undisclosed documents to Defence witnesses on cross-examination, and -- and it is my understanding that the issue arose repeatedly during the trial, was the subject of a number of oral decisions, this being just the first of them. In any event, I would submit that even under this test we should be allowed to put the documents to the witness, and I would draw the attention to -- on page 5, the Court's attention to the last paragraph that is quoted from the Hadzihasanovic decision there where it says: "In the opinion of the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution may present in the course of its cross-examination any documents that have not already been admitted in order to test the credibility of a witness or to refresh such a witness's memory. In each of these two cases the Prosecution may present a document that has not already been admitted and which it had in its possession before or after presentation of its case." Now, it's true, as Mr. Mansfield alluded, in that decision -- it's not quoted here, but the Court imposed a 24-hour disclosure rule in that case. I would -- I would submit that this Court should not follow that rule, and the -- there's no such rule provided for in the Rutaganda decision. Clearly in that decision the material was provided, as in this case, at the close of the direct examination and there was no problem with that. There was no problem with notice. There was no problem whatsoever with the Prosecution putting those documents to the witness. And therefore, I think this Court should follow the Rutaganda decision rather than the Hadzihasanovic decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it not a simple matter of fairness, if we reach the point, about the use of the document that you submit? The question of whether some delay is required is a matter of fairness, is it not, and that might vary case by case, particular document by document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I can -- I can imagine a situation where the -- it is conceivable to me that fairness might require earlier disclosure. I'm not sure. In other words, I cannot -- I can appreciate that it may be -- this may be a case-by-case issue. However, I would say that a blanket rule or even an inclination to have prior disclosure is unwise because until the Prosecution actually hears the witness's evidence, it's not -- it's not very -- it's not clear what is going to be important and what is not, and it's impossible to anticipate all the issues that are going to arise, all the things that the witness is going to say, how they might become relevant, how they might become important, and it would be extremely difficult if not impossible for the Prosecution to try to anticipate every issue that might arise in the witness's examination-in-chief that it would have to then -- it would then have to rebut before the examination even begins. This is a good example of that. Mr. Mansfield cited the pre-trial brief and the witness's 65 ter summary. Well, to get down in the details here, the document that I would like to put to the witness deals -- the sections that I would like to put to the witness deal primarily with the March-April 1998 period. That period is not even addressed in the pre-trial brief of the accused some of the there no discussion about that at all. It goes immediately from coming to Kosovo, jumping all the way right to the 9th of May. With respect to the 65 ter summary for this -- for the accused, it is one page long, not detailed, and on this issue the only thing it says is that -- is that he established a Celiku 1 unit in Klecka. No date, no context, no time frame, and in fact it's a little unclear whether that's what he said in his testimony. I think his testimony is considerably more ambiguous on that subject, at least with respect to the March-April time period. So to be fair, it was only when the witness testified about that period and about the structure in detail that it became something that even if I had had it beforehand, which I didn't, in translation, I don't think I would have -- it would have jumped out as something I necessarily would have wanted to use. So I think that that this is a -- this is a good example why there can't be a bright-line rule about disclosure before the witness testifies because it's impossible to know what might arise. I mean, well, not impossible, but it's impossible to know all of the aspects and all the dimensions of what the witness's testimony is going to be. So I think that both for the legal reasons which are set forth in the Rutaganda decision and for the particular factual reasons which I have set forth with respect to this document, I think that we should be allowed to put the document to the witness in cross-examination in order to challenge his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, you accept that it was made available in the course of Thursday afternoon to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And could you just put your submission on why this shouldn't have been disclosed as part of your Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's -- I don't think it's -- it's not a document that we -- that we wanted to rely on as our Prosecution case. Not because of reliability reasons but we don't -- we don't know necessarily who all the authors are of the document, to what extent we could have authenticated it. And with respect to the principal issues in this case, Lapusnik, it touches on that, but as I said, it's more -- it's more directly relevant to the March-April time period which has more significance now that the -- now that Mr. Limaj has testified. So it's -- it's a document that we had looked at without translating it. We didn't get the translation until more recently, but it was a document that we simply chose -- not because we didn't think it was -- not because we thought it was unreliable, but simply we chose not -- not to put it in. And also, we draw certain limits on all the open-source material that we're going to put in. We can't put in all relevant open-source material. But it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm left a little confused. Are you saying you recognised its potential relevance but chose not to use it? Or are you saying you didn't realise its potential relevance because it was not translated? Or are you saying some other thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What I'm saying is something in between, actually. We took a quick look at the document, at the book, without having an interpreter look at the book quickly, determined that there were -- there was no discussion about the crimes charged in this case, decided for that reason that we weren't going to pursue it any further. We later on looked at the book again and decided out of interest and potential relevance to translate about ten different chapters of the book. Each chapter is a short summary of a person's life, and then when those translations came back in the last week and in light of the testimony of the accused, it became apparent to us that there are passages in the document, in the book, which are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, if I may, shortly. The last observations, if we may put it this way, don't really make any sense at all. From the beginning of this case, the period of March and April was known to be of crucial importance. It was opened by all sides as having importance both by the Prosecution and by ourselves on behalf of Mr. Limaj, and Mr. Limaj himself in an extensive opening. The book makes clear -- one only has to look at tab 3, bottom of page. It's dealing with March 1998, Ismet Jashari and Fatmir is mentioned, Fatmir Limaj, on the second or penultimate line of that page. So it must be extremely clear from a very early stage that it had relevant material in it. So therefore there isn't a clear answer as to why it wasn't used before. The fact that it wasn't translated until recently we say doesn't really hold water if it's relevant and reliable. May I just turn to the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The more pertinent issue may be why it wasn't disclosed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, why it wasn't disclosed earlier, that being a document which they may have been slow to translate, but we certainly should have been alerted to it whether they were going to rely on it or not, in fact, whether they were going to rely on it under the disclosure rules. As far as the fairness if I may take that point up. What the Prosecution is saying we've been rather tardy in translating it. Sorry about that. We weren't going to rely on it anyway really because we don't know yet and we didn't know. However we're not going to give anybody an opportunity to consider it before we cross-examine. We find, if I may put it, the height of unfairness because the one theme of the cases in relation to these matters, if they are admissible and you may recall that in putting this matter to Your Honours I accepted that there might be exceptions as a route to admissibility, one of them being credibility, but the theme underlying the admission of material under that heading of the cases is the opportunity for the person to assimilate and familiarise himself with the materials. May I just point out paragraph 282 in the Rutaganda decision which you have in front of you, whereby "The record shows that at the start of the cross-examination of the Appellant, the Prosecution presented the Chamber with a file containing documents that it intended to use during cross-examination. The three documents cited by the appellant were also within the file and had not been previously disclosed to the Defence. The Trial Chamber permitted the Prosecution to tender them, but in order to allow the appellant time to familiarise himself with the materials postponed questioning on them until the next day." Now, that's all one saying here, that if in fact leaving the aside the question of disclosure in principle they are admissible under this heading, then even that court was saying there has to be time for a witness, in this case a defendant, to familiarise himself. And in fact 291 in the same report makes the same point: "It should be recalled the Trial Chamber accorded the appellant sufficient time to familiarise himself with the photographs, the press clipping, and articles of association." The fact that it appears the opportunity wasn't taken is another matter. So that's clearly underlying that decision. And may I just hand up. We have copies of the Hadzihasanovic decision. I don't know if the Prosecution have it. If they don't there's another one here. We did inform the Prosecution about this. There's one for each. Just -- sorry. There's one amendment that was amended orally, and it's rather important. It comes at -- I'm sorry, the individual pages are not numbered, but page 12524 is in the middle of a page a few pages in, about six, I think, six --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Page 3 of 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm obliged. And on the following actual page, at line 22 -- they're different here, yes. It's different again. Well, may I -- there's a wording which should read "cannot" instead of "can only." May I hand it up separately in a moment? It doesn't affect the point I'm just about to make. The point in this particular decision -- may I just pause for a moment? I'm sorry. I'm afraid there are three different copies of this. Effectively what this authority is saying - I concede obviously there will be a series of these decisions, but - is exactly the same, and it is this one that has an indication very clearly that there should be -- well, they set down 24 hours, but I'm not suggesting it always has to be 24 hours. It's page 12527. 12527. It's dealt with in more than one place, but it is there dealing, line 4, where the category of testing credibility is set out, and it must disclose, line 10, such a document to the Defence and its intention to use such a document, line 12, "at least 24 hours before a Defence witness appears," and so on. And therefore, we say whilst it may not be a firm rule that it has to be 24 hours, what is clear from both of these two is that the Court is saying, in fairness, the witness must have this opportunity. It may be measured as 24 hours. It may be measured as overnight, but at least time -- of course it will differ because some documents are very short and you can look at them in five minutes. But this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In that decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- it seems to be put as 24 hours before a Defence witness appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I quickly have read the other decisions, were they not speaking of 24 hours before cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, it's not entirely clear. But I -- from the -- the other authority, the Rutaganda authority, plainly looking at the facts of it, they're really saying, since the way it has arisen exactly as this one has, we'll give the witness overnight, so an interval of time when the witness is already in the witness box. And all I'm saying is that, as I say, leaving aside the issue much disclosure in principle which we say should have happened here anyway which would have allowed him plenty of time to have a look at it. But if in fact none of that has been adhered to he should be now allowed an opportunity before he's asked any questions. That's all we're asking for. And if it's overnight - I don't suppose Mr. Whiting intends to finish today - at least we should have or someone should have permission to provide him with a copy of the document without comment so he can have a look at it overnight. We say that's a basic fairness principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know you don't want tennis matches, but just on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The French Open is on. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But just two small points. The first is with respect to disclosure, I don't think this document was required to be disclosed under the Rules, under either 66(A)(i) or 66(B) or 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought you dealt with disclosure earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Fine, then. But with providing it to the witness, I certainly have no objection with the document being given to Mr. Limaj and him having an opportunity overnight to read the document and consider it. I'm not intending -- it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that practical? Are you intending to lead off with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I had no intention. It's no problem to put it off until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We will take a few moments to deal with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I did-

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Mansfield. I didn't give a further shot at the ball.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No. It's just the correction. It's a rather important correction. It appears on page 4 of 8 which is the copy you have. I'm sorry it's taken a little time to locate it. On page 4 of 8, at line 22 it says, "As a result of this principle the Prosecution can only present in the course of cross-examination..." In fact, the wording which was amended in an oral decision on the 2nd of December, 2004, I can give the reference, that was amended to "cannot present in the course of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. its cross-examination." So it is rather an important amendment. And we have a copy of the amendment for Your Honours as well if you would like to have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We accept what you have put, Mr. Mansfield. We will adjourn now for a short time. --- Break taken at 3.04 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that there can be no objection in principle to the use of this material as cross-examination going to credit of the witness. The decision of the Appeals Chamber in the decision from Rwanda of Rutaganda and the decision of the Trial Chamber in Hadzihasanovic and Kubura are directly, it seems to us, in point and deal with the matter of principle. The arguments considered in Rutaganda appear in essence to be those advanced by way of objection here. There remains a question of whether some special measures should be taken as matter of fairness. We are of the view that they should, and conscious of the indication of Mr. Whiting that it won't be until tomorrow afternoon that this matter is reached. From what we presently understand of the matter, that would appear to be an appropriate delay to deal with the matter of fairness. We would observe that the reference in the decision to which we were also referred of the Trial Chamber in Hadzihasanovic, which suggested that it would be necessary for material of this nature to be made available a time before the witness entered the witness box appears to us to misread the effect of the Appeals Chamber decision in Rutaganda, and while it may have been an appropriate measure in that particular case, it's certainly not one which is established as a minimum requirement. We do, however, think that there should be some further indication given on the basis of fairness; that is, that the witness having an opportunity to read this material overnight, and for that purpose a copy should be provided to Mr. Limaj at the close of evidence today. When his cross-examination has concluded and before any re-examination, in the view of the Chamber he should have an opportunity to instruct his counsel in respect only of the content of this material. And if as a consequence of those instructions there is any reason for some change of the timetable, well, then that can be raised then. So basically yes, the material may be used now. It will be provided to Mr. Limaj this evening at the close of our sitting so that he can consider it overnight and before we commence tomorrow. And at the it end of his cross-examination, given that by arrangement between counsel he is not being spoken to by his counsel during his evidence, that should be relaxed, his counsel have an opportunity to take instructions and do that before re-examination arises. We will commence now, then, Mr. Whiting, with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could just inquire, did the brief adjournment restart the lock, the hour and a half clock, or will we need to adjourn at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It did not restart the clock. You will be adjourning at about twenty-five minutes to 30 minutes from now, bearing in mind that we had a start that was just after twenty past two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can plan to have no more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll do my best and somebody will tug at my sleeve if I fail to notice the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I'm going to start where you finished off in your direct examination, when you told the Chamber that when you learned of the indictment against you from this Tribunal and you were contacted by the media you lied about where you were. That's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already gave the reasons why I maintained the approach I did towards media, why I didn't tell them the place I was. And I don't consider that a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you explain to me why telling the press that you were in Austria or Italy or some other place when in fact you were in Slovenia is not a lie? Put aside the justifications that you gave. It was not the truth; right, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because after the war, I participated in the political developments, and I know how an official should behave. The contacts had already started between Mr. Steiner and the Prime Minister. I didn't want the media to know my whereabouts before the official -- an official statement was made, because I knew that the media representatives would come to my hotel and they would ask me. That was the first indictment made against a KLA member in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And because you did not want the media to -- or because you say you did not want the media to come to your hotel, you lied about where you were; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already stated that in my opinion, this cannot be proved as a lie as you are saying. For me, that was simply my private approach, not to tell them where I was for the moment, because I deemed it best, in my interest and in the interest of further developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you didn't tell them that you refused to tell them. You didn't say, "I refuse to tell you where I am." You told them something that was not true. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have told the truth to the persons whom I should tell the truth: The representatives of the UN General-Secretary, and your office is part of that. For me that was more important than telling the media where I was. Mr. Steiner knew where I was. Your office knew where I was. The Prime Minister of Kosova knew where I was, and for me that was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So is it your testimony when -- that when you deem it in your best interests you can decide who you tell the truth to and who you don't tell the truth to? Is that your testimony, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not so. But I tried to abide by the principle of official posts, because I was an official of the parliament of Kosova and of a political party. That's why I have tried to follow that logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you were a public figure, as you testified, starting from 2000 approximately; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from 2000. Starting from the end of 1998 and onwards I was always -- maybe not always. Less so in 1988 to 1989. But from 1989 I was always present in the media, especially after the opening of the television stations in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, 1998. Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And from 1998 on was it normal your practice when speaking to the media to be untruthful?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. I think I am one of the personalities who was always transparent to the media. This can be proven by all the media outlets in Kosova, both Albanian and otherwise. I don't think there has ever been a more transparent and willing spokesperson to talk to the media and tell the media the truth. I have even made the difference between my personal view and the personal view of the party, and you can verify that with all the media, print and electronic media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you tried to be truthful with the media.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always. Always.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me take you back to 1996 when you joined the KLA. I believe you testified that you joined in August of 1996; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You joined with Rexhep Selimi.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't join with him, by said it was through Rexhep Selimi that I joined. I said that my first contact was with Rexhep Selimi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Rexhep Selimi was a member of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rexhep Selimi I heard was a member of the General Staff, as a member, a full member, in November. But as a representative of the General Staff, I heard that he was such in March when we came from Switzerland. It was then that he introduced himself as a representative. But as a full member I found out that it was in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's March of 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference between the representative of the General Staff and a full member. As a representative of the General Staff, it was in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said March, and that's March of 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a representative of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On your first day of testimony, you were asked if in 1996 -- 1996, after you joined the KLA, you assisted with any guerrilla actions and you said that you didn't have the opportunity then. That's your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Then in 1997 you went to Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that you had no contact with the KLA during your time in Switzerland. That's your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to explain here, Your Honours. The people with whom -- whom had contacts with the KLA, who purchased -- who raised money on behalf of the KLA were numerous in Switzerland. But in my opinion, they were not members of the KLA as such in Switzerland. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you were not receiving any instructions from the KLA at that time. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that you had contact with Homeland Calling and the Kosovo Popular Movement for Switzerland but not with the KLA. You shook your head yes. Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened with the KLA in November of 1997?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When the KLA became public in a way at a funeral.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall who the funeral was for?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in November 1997, there was a football match -- there was a clash between guerrilla unit of the KLA Llausha village and the Serb forces, and during the fighting the Serb forces killed a teacher of the village, Halil Geci was his name if I'm not wrong. And his funeral which took place after two days with the participation of a large number citizens, it was the first time that three members of the KLA appeared before the gathering of people, and they read a speech or an address to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: One of those members was Rexhep Selimi.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we found that out much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you recall giving an interview in the summer of 2000 that is in evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't give an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't give an interview in the summer of 2000?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What -- what interview do you mean? Because I know that I have given a lot of interviews to newspapers and to television stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's a televised interview, and it's in evidence in this case as P -- Exhibit P36. It's been shown in this trial. Do you recall your answering questions about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already told you that I have given many interviews, and I don't understand which of them do you mean. And of course during my interviews, I have spoken also about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll show you a part of this interview. If we could look at clip 4, which starts on page 6 of Prosecution Exhibit P36. And I think we switch to Sanction for this. If we could switch to Sanction, please. Mr. Limaj, if you could just listen carefully.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] It's interesting. Sometime around 1996, we were going to go out to carry out an operation. That was our duty. And I was waiting for the now Minister of Public Order, Rexhep Selimi, to come. And we had set a time. But there was a barber there, a neighbour of behind from the village, and I was waiting for him to come because it was our meeting place. And from the conversation that was going on at the barber shop, the talk was about the KLA at that time was still not much talked about. And they started to discuss among themselves how many Serbs -- and who was behind them, and what was going on, whether the Serbs killing them for various reasons. I don't know what, a wide debate. "In the course of this somebody asked me directly, What do you think about this army. He asked me rather because I stay in Pristina then maybe I knew more than he did. Then nature of our operation was very secret, and it was very hard for me indeed to tell him. But I found an answer. I said, Listen, if the Serbs have been inventing us, it is to our good. If it's the Serbs who are in fact doing this, we must still support it. Because they are damaging themselves by doing it. "Interviewer: That is very true. 26 November 1997 was perhaps the first time that an organised KLA was launched. "What do you think of the case of Mitrovica? "Fatmir Limaj: In fact, the condition for all the success of the KLA, or rather the military leadership, throughout the war was that it was able at certain moments to move from one phase of action to the other. At the most suitable moments it moved from one phase to the next. The case of Ludoviq is connected to this. Until then the KLA had made a deep secret of its operations. But it took a difficult step that it would have been hard for other organisation to do, moving from a profound underground conspiracy to a public appearance in war. This was indeed a step that was as brave as it was dangerous. "Interviewer: What do you remember -- How do you remember Ludoviq? "Fatmir Limaj: I was not present at Ludoviq because I was abroad. I was in Switzerland on other duties assigned to me by the General Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, did you see in that view that sometime in 1996 you were waiting for Rexhep Selimi to carry out an operation? You nodded your head yes. That was true; right? That happened in 1996?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said but I was not present in the action. This proves precisely what I said earlier, that Rexhep Selimi -- I offered an opportunity to Rexhep Selimi not only to him but to KLA to use my home in my native village for various reasons. In this interview, Rexhep Selimi was at my home and I went there to receive him. They came from an action and I took them in. That was the assistance I gave to him and to KLA. And this proves what I have told you so far. You asked me directly whether I participated in some operation. I did not. The answer is I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So Mr. Limaj, you said in this interview at some time in 1996, "We were to go" -- we -- "We were to go out and carry out an operation. That was our task. I was waiting for Rexhep Selimi." Your testimony is you were not involved in this operation? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, Mr. Prosecutor, if you want to make distinction that's your problem. I have always felt I belonged to the KLA as of August, and whatever I said I was part of it. But in answer to your direct question whether I participated in some operations in 1996, the answer is no. The only thing is that I received Rexhep Selimi together with a friend of his in my home and in this way I rendered my contribution. But it was not a direct contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's what you were trying to say when you said, "We were to go out and carry out an operation"? That's what you were trying to say there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I told you what I wanted to say. I think I was clear. Even in the interview it is clear. You may interpret it in the way you wish but I think it's very clear and straightforward as I'm telling you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that will be up to the Court decide. But you also say in this interview -- you also say in this interview that you were not at -- at Ludoviq because you had been tasked -- you were in Switzerland for some duties that you had been tasked with by the General Staff. And that's true, isn't it, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those who worked for the Homeland Calls felt an obligation to raise funds, and I -- I meant there that all my activity was an ongoing activity. All the activists who were involved in fund-raising in Switzerland and in other western countries were, of course, did this on behalf of the General Staff. The General Staff, then the central staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you testified in this courtroom last week and again today that you had not been given any tasks by the General Staff in Switzerland, that in fact you weren't even in contact with the General Staff. Here in this interview you say that you were given tasks -- assigned tasks by the General Staff. Which one is true, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is what I'm telling you now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So again in this interview you lied. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you have in front of you a person who lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Again, that will be up to the Court. Is that your only answer?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let Their Honours give it the weight it deserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You don't acknowledge that what you said in this interview is not true? You're unable to acknowledge that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not telling you that this is not true. I'm trying to explain to you that in the interview I say we have been assigned by the General Staff because at that time this is how everybody saw it, assigned by the General Staff. When we left Kosova, we act in cooperation with the people who were working for Kosova, who did everything on behalf of the General Staff. So when I say that we were assigned by the General Staff meant this, what I'm saying now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you think both things are true, what you said in your interview and what you said in court here today?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain to you the general context, to explain what in reality I wanted to say or what I imply when I say I was assigned by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What you wanted to say is that in that first interview, you wanted people to believe, true or not, that you were involved in the KLA. In court here, you want people to believe that was not the case. Isn't that true, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, on the contrary. Your Honours, the day before yesterday, I said that I received a message from Rexhep Selimi in the middle of 1997 after some separation. He followed my activity, and he wanted me to continue my activity through this Homeland Calls. It was a kind of approval by Mr. Selimi about what I was doing there, because I had time to prove my ability and valour during my future actions. I left Kosova, was involved in this Homeland Calls association, and this is what happened and what I told you during the other days. It's not the purpose as the Prosecutor alleges that I wanted the citizens to believe that, because the citizens know very well my CV. I have openly declared what I was and what I've been doing. And this interview was given certainly to the foreign media. You should bear that in mind. It aimed also at showing -- proving a certain continuity in our organisation, because that interview was not meant for the local media and to -- and for me to take pride before the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So in other words you could say one thing to the foreign media and something else to the people in Kosovo? Is that what you're saying, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's what it sounded like.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may sound like that to you, but it's not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, Mr. Limaj, are you now telling us -- initially you said that you thought your tasks with homeland security [sic] were somehow tasked by the KLA. Are you now telling us that that letter from Rexhep Selimi was a tasking, what you meant when you said you had been assigned to do work for the General Staff? Is that your testimony now?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the question is rather long, sir, so I don't know what to answer first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, Mr. Limaj. The -- initially when I put this question to you, you said that you thought that homeland -- working for homeland -- I almost said homeland security -- Homeland Calling was being tasked by the KLA. Now you have said -- as I've pressed you on this matter, you've talked about this letter from Rexhep Selimi. Are you saying that this letter was a tasking or an assignment from the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are putting it in this way. I am telling you different things. Maybe you want me to say this. I received a message from Mr. Selimi after I had left Kosova and gone to Albania after the developments. I received a message by him in the form of a greeting telling me, Do what you are doing, continue what you are doing. Send us money because we need the money. You may interpret it as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a friendly greeting and an appreciation of what I was doing in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So it was not a tasking or assignment. Yes or no, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I wanted to tell you. I have no other answer. This was only an encouragement for the good work, what we were doing. And wherever we went to raise money, we told the people in exile, I mean the people, diaspora, we told them that we are raising this money on behalf of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The truth is, Mr. Limaj, that depending on who you're talking to you tell a different truth that's more convenient for you. Isn't that right, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next topic is lengthy, so perhaps this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will take the break now and resume at ten minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, let's go back in time. You testified that as early as 1990 there was not a single person who wasn't following up developments very closely in Kosovo; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I think. I think that it was the case with the majority of Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that in 1996, at the time you joined the KLA, you became aware of communiques that were being published by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I said was that I got acquainted with the KLA before the communiques, and this was sometime in 1995 or 1996. This is when I first heard about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you became aware of the communiques before you joined the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the daily media. I think there was one or two communiques published. I'm not quite sure. I think before I got engaged in the KLA, there were two communiques published in the daily press, and this was before I got engaged in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you went to Switzerland, of course you continued to pay attention to events in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You read the communiques that were issued during 1997?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You knew that the KLA saw itself as a liberation army and not as a terrorist organisation. Right, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You knew that the KLA saw the Serbs as the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think that it saw the Serbs as terrorists but saw the Milosevic regime as the occupying force, as an occupying regime. As an occupying force that was exercising violence. I don't think that "terrorists" can be used in that context. Occupying is more -- a more adequate word. We always used to fight against the Serb terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You knew that the KLA talked about the occupying regime as terrorists. Yes?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said, as a terrorist, barbaric regime. There were different terms used, and not only by the KLA but the majority of Albanians applied these different terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You knew that the KLA was seeking international support for its cause; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You knew that to get support, international support, the KLA had to show that it was not a terrorist organisation but that it was a regular, organised army; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The KLA wanted to show more that it was a liberation force. And not only before the international community but before the community in the country itself, that it was a liberation army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Not just --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A liberating army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Not just a liberating army but an organised, orderly army; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This became a KLA objective later on, to present itself as an organised army. But at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was one of the goals of the KLA to become an organised army so that it could get international support. Isn't that right, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that things were different at that time. At that time, we were running the risk, Your Honour, for the KLA to be called a terrorist organisation. And at that time, you cannot call a terrorist organisation on the basis of its organisation. We do have terrorist organisations that are well organised. At that time, the KLA wanted to make clear its activities. That had nothing to do with terrorist activities, as I said. We do have many organised, well-organised organisations which are terrorist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You wanted to show the world that the KLA was an army with popular support; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depending on the period of time you're referring to, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me specify. After Prekaz, the KLA had popular support; right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Prekaz, yes. It began there. The Prekaz events was the key to what happened later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was a turning point.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. I think that Prekaz is the turning point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also knew -- and that was the beginning of March 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Prekaz, that's the beginning of March 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This occurred on the 5th, 6th, and 7th of March after the events in Qirez and Likoshan, which happened, if I'm not mistaken, on the 28th or 29th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also knew that the KLA saw Ibrahim Rugova's policies as a failure; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this period things were really confusing. It is true that the KLA at that time appealed for unity, because every organisation tends and has an objective to be popular. But the situation was confusing because the KLA at that time was a small group, and above all we were thinking of remaining in underground. We thought that they shouldn't come out in public --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you because I don't think you're answering the question. The question was: The KLA thought that Rugova's approach was a failure; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The KLA thought that the political attempts until that time failed and that it should search for another alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the political attempts, to be clear, were the attempts that were being promoted by Ibrahim Rugova; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not promoted by Ibrahim Rugova but promoted by different political bodies. Ibrahim Rugova was just one of these different political bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But he was one of the ones promoting it and probably the most prominent and the KLA thought that his approach was a failure; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to give you the real picture at that time, these things need to be clarified. For at that time you can say yes, that Ibrahim Rugova was the promoter of such a policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you also thought that Rugova's approach was a failure; right? You yourself.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't think so that, but this was obvious in every step that you made. I was sure that this way could not lead us to anything concrete, to any changes for Kosova. And such messages were received by the international community as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand your answer. You said, "No, I didn't think that," but then you said it was obvious. Did you think it was a failure or not, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe my answer was confusing, but what I meant was that this is what I thought, and this is what was obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. You also knew that the KLA had a policy of targeting people suspected of collaborating; right? You knew that.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The KLA aimed at targeting those who were directly working for the Serbian police and secret service. There was a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. communique issued to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall which communique that was?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I'm maybe not sure. Such communiques appeared in 1996 and even later, but I can't tell you exactly which.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at the communiques and see if we can find that one you described, because I don't recall seeing it. But you claimed on the second day of testimony and you've repeated it to some extent just now, that for the KLA, "collaborators were," and I'm quoting you, "were those people who were actively inspectors in the UDB or in the police, people directly involved in operations involving murders, assassination attempts, offences or ransacking and searches, violation, imprisonment of people, persistent operations." That's what you said was how the KLA defined collaborators; right? Is that yes?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is how I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in -- from early 1997, Jakup Krasniqi was on the General Staff of the KLA; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. For the first time I saw Jakup Krasniqi as a member, as a spokesperson of the KLA of General Staff when he appeared publicly. I didn't know that before. I didn't even know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So as of June 14, 1998, you knew that he was on the General Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a spokesperson of the General Staff, and normally he necessarily should be a member in the capacity of the spokesperson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that after the 14th of June you saw Jakup Krasniqi regularly. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the 14th of June, I used to see him quite frequently when he came to Klecke. I went to his home at a later time. Once I saw him in Kroimire. Yes, I did see him frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in fact you said that you met with him at least every other day after the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When he was in Klecke, I saw him in Divjak. I'm saying Klecke, but Divjak. I saw him on a daily basis almost. But he didn't stay all the time in Divjak and Klecke. He went to different places. But for the time he was in Klecke or in Divjak in his base I saw him regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified that you went to him with demands because you needed to have, and I'm quoting you, you "needed to have available more accurate information as to what we should do from now then -- onwards." That's your testimony, isn't it, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that happened for the first time officially when I said you could address a KLA General Staff representative. In this case I thought that through him everything could be resolved, because after 29th of May, as I said, events changed the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, you said that he -- you described him as "the most competent person with which we could discuss issues directly." Those were the words you used on the second day of your testimony. You're nodding your head. Now, he defined collaborators very differently from the way you've defined collaborators in this courtroom. He defined -- he testified that collaborators were people who caused the country damage. He said a collaborator is a person who "was harmful to the KLA, when such a person is giving information on the movements of the KLA to the Belgrade regime." That's how he defined collaborators, Mr. Limaj. And that's what you thought, too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Facts speak differently. They prove what I am saying. If what you are saying is true, then the KLA would have never found the support of the large masses of people, and it would be likely turned into a terrorist organisation. I have thought what I have stated here before this Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you saying that you had a different view than the KLA or that Mr. Krasniqi was wrong about how he described collaborators?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that I have seen what the KLA did, and this is how I saw it. As to Mr. Krasniqi, he may have given, issued confusing statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi also said at another point in his testimony that -- he talked about "collaborators of the enemy who are numerous in Kosovo in the economic and the political sphere as well as the cultural and in the security spheres." That's again a much broader definition of collaborators than what you offered in court here in your testimony, isn't it, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a difference, but I think we must make things clear here. You are asking me whether the target of the KLA were the collaborators, those whom I referred to here as people who have collaborated with the Serb. But those who have worked with the Serbs, they are different from the collaborators. At least this is how I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question for you is: Was your view different from the KLA's view?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not different. I'm telling you I have seen from the concrete actions of the KLA. I'm not claiming here that any mistakes might not have been made, but the actions of the KLA during 1996, 1997 were what I'm trying to tell here. Some mistakes may have been committed, but the KLA had clear instructions as to the people who they might target through communiques. I think that we have acted along the logic that the KLA followed, which coincides with my logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, that answer gives rise to a number of questions. The first is: You said the KLA followed this approach during 1996, 1997. You didn't say anything about 1998. Did something change in 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was it the same in 1998 according to you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said 1996 in the sense of how I came to form such a vision, things which enabled me to create the opinion that I have. That's why I referred to 1996 and 1997. I think that it was at this time that the KLA dealt with such persons, but this continued, of course, during 1998, 1999, at least as far as the policy of the KLA is concerned. People may have erred, but I can't say. We cannot say this was the policy followed by the KLA. Sometimes the KLA itself, the General Staff, has made some mistakes. Such mistakes cannot be ruled out, but I'm speaking in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But just to be clear, your testimony is that the KLA's policy was to target collaborators who were actively working for the Serb police or UDB in 1996, 1997, and 1998? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the target of the KLA in 1996, 1997, 1998 were the people who were - not necessarily in 1996 but even before that time - people who were active and participated in murders, violations, kidnapping, and indirect massacres committed by the Serbs. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also testified just a moment ago that the KLA had "clear instructions as to the people who they might target through communiques." Is it your testimony that those clear instructions were communicated through the communiques or by some other means?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, Your Honours, that through the communiques the KLA had made clear its objective, its approach, and through its operations on the ground during the murder of these inspectors. So through the communique you could understand who the target of the KLA actions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So when you referred to "clear instructions" you were only referring to the communiques. Is that right, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, only to the concrete actions that could be seen on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krasniqi, who testified here and who was responsible for some of those communiques, testified that never in those communiques was there a definition provided as to what was a collaborator. And that's true, isn't it, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying to explain things. If you are asking me whether the communiques contained in writing in explicit terms who should be killed and who shouldn't, this is not true. But the communiques proved that a collaborator, an inspector, was killed because of his activity. Another thing: In the region that person lived the citizens knew very well who he was because otherwise the citizens would have responded against his murder. This is what I'm telling you, not that the communiques contained written statements to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So in other words your testimony is that the KLA counted on people knowing who the specific individuals named in the communiques were and they were in fact people who had worked for the police or UDB. Because that was never stated in the communiques that they had worked for the police or the UDB, was it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have the communiques in front of you. They say that Enver Bajgora is a UDB inspector who directly participated in murders, raids and -- his is no better information than to tell you that Enver Bajgora was killed. A police inspector was killed. I don't remember the place. And you have other occasions like this. This is a concrete example to show the activity of such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember any other examples from the communiques?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lutfi Havazi, another example. If I'm not mistaken he was injured, a man who had clearly participated in political assassination attempts, massacres. One of my colleagues in Kosova - I heard it here - Sabri Hamiti was injured by this person, together with another person. Or the murder of Enver Maloku. It turned out that Lutfi Havazi had prepared that murder act. Sabri Hamiti, a distinguished academician, that too was perpetrated by him. And there are enigmatic injuries of persons who are discussed even now in Kosova. And there are other instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you think of any other examples where the communique identified somebody as being a police inspector or a member of the UDB and was killed for that reason?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to remember each and every one, Your Honours. Apart from Lutfi Havazi, maybe Zymer Zymeri. An assassination attempt was staged but it failed. He too had directly participated in the preparation of such operations against these peoples who are still a mystery. The testimony given by the UDB inspector shows that -- I read that testimony. Your Honours, there are many such instances which I personally may not know because the activity in the UDB, as we have seen even here, was kept confidential. Some people knew about that but not everyone. The Prosecutor's office could have brought us the files to see who they were, those people who had directly participated in such actions. I'm just citing only some cases which are public knowledge, concrete cases which show clearly what the orientation is, the direction which we should go and which we have gone. I'm not telling that mistakes were not made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, are you now saying that in some instances collaborators were killed because they were secretly part of the police?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The bulk of them, those who were murdered, had taken concrete actions. But I mean that there are other people whose activity we don't know, who have been involved in various operations, but we can't know all of them. As the case is with Lutfi Havazi whose activity is not known for the public in Kosova. It was here that I heard about the murder of Lutfi Maloku [as interpreted] by that person. Many people in Kosova to this day do not know that he was the one who did it. I think that the KLA knew what it was doing in the concrete instances since it has undertaken such operations against such individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's completely untrue, isn't it, Mr. Limaj? Let's talk about Ramiz Hoxha and Selman Binici.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know that they were killed by the KLA on the 2nd of October, 1998; right? You're nodding.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ramiz Hoxha was from Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Selman Binici was from Banje?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The 2nd of October, 1998, those villages were within the 121st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please, the last part of it?
